stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar. A 34 year old G2P1 woman at 26+3 weeks gestation attends for review of her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Her previous baby weighed 4.4 kg at 39 weeks and was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery; she had no formal diabetes testing in that pregnancy. She has a BMI of 33 and her mother has type 2 diabetes.

Her 75 g OGTT results are fasting 4.9 mmol/L (fasting under 5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (1 hour under 10.0), 2 hour 8.4 mmol/L (2 hour under 8.5). Her booking HbA1c was 5.4 percent (under 5.7 percent), booking bloods otherwise normal. Her blood pressure today is 118/72 mmHg and urinalysis shows no glycosuria and no proteinuria. Foetal growth on symphysis-fundal height measurement is on the 75th percentile.

She asks whether the results are normal, and what happens next.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): Fasting 4.9 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hour 8.4 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Examination: BP 118/72 mmHg, no glycosuria, no proteinuria, SFH on 75th centile

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Order fasting insulin and HbA1c today to distinguish gestational from pre-existing diabetes
options.rationale: Insulin measurement is not part of GDM diagnostic testing and adds no management value; the ADIPS OGTT thresholds define the diagnosis (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

options.text: Reassure her the test is normal and continue routine antenatal care visits
options.rationale: Only her fasting and 2 hour values are under threshold; the 1 hour value of 10.6 mmol/L exceeds 10.0 mmol/L and diagnoses GDM under ADIPS criteria (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

options.text: Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks at 30 weeks because only one value is abnormal
options.rationale: The ADIPS diagnosis needs only one abnormal value; repeat testing is not indicated and delays management that reduces macrosomia (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg orally twice daily now without further monitoring or education
options.rationale: Initial GDM management is lifestyle and blood glucose monitoring for 1 to 2 weeks; pharmacotherapy is added only if targets are not met and needs monitoring set-up first (Source: ADIPS GDM Management Statement).

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and refer to the antenatal diabetes clinic for education
options.rationale: The ADIPS criteria diagnose gestational diabetes when any one value is met or exceeded; her 1 hour value of 10.6 mmol/L exceeds the 10.0 mmol/L threshold and requires referral to the antenatal diabetes clinic (Source: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM).
source_refs: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

explanation.summary: Australian universal screening at 24 to 28 weeks uses a 75 g OGTT with ADIPS diagnostic thresholds: fasting 5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L. A single value at or above threshold diagnoses GDM. Management starts with lifestyle (dietitian input, home glucose monitoring 4 times daily) with targets fasting under 5.0 and postprandial 1 hour under 7.4 or 2 hour under 6.7. Metformin then insulin are added if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks. Delivery timing balances glycaemic control and foetal size, with induction at 38 to 39 weeks if insulin required or macrosomia identified.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L
A single abnormal value diagnoses GDM
First step is education, monitoring and lifestyle for 1 to 2 weeks
Metformin then insulin if targets are not met
Universal 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks in Australia
explanation.pearls: Early screening (14 to 20 weeks) is offered for BMI at least 35, prior GDM, prior macrosomic baby over 4.5 kg, first degree relative with diabetes, or high risk ethnicity.

sources.label: ADIPS 75 g OGTT Diagnostic Criteria for GDM

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgery for tubal ectopic in a woman with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 29 year old G3P1 woman presents at 6+4 weeks gestation by dates with 3 days of intermittent right sided lower abdominal ache and light spotting. She had a right salpingectomy 2 years ago for a ruptured tubal ectopic. She is trying to conceive and this is her first pregnancy since the surgery.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable. Vital signs are pulse 82, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Abdominal palpation reveals mild left iliac fossa tenderness with no guarding or rebound. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity with a 22 mm complex left adnexal mass adjacent to but separate from the left ovary, containing a small yolk sac with no foetal pole and no foetal cardiac activity; there is a small volume of anechoic fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

Beta hCG is 3200 IU/L, done today, with a value of 3150 IU/L 48 hours ago. She has normal renal, liver and full blood count results, and is very keen to preserve her fertility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding, no rebound
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterine cavity; left adnexal mass 22 mm with yolk sac, no foetal pole, no cardiac activity; small anechoic fluid in pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 3200 IU/L today, 3150 IU/L 48 hours ago; renal, liver and FBC normal
data_table.Surgical history: Right salpingectomy 2 years ago for ruptured tubal ectopic

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Single dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscular with day 4 and day 7 beta hCG follow-up
options.rationale: Although this ectopic meets biochemical and imaging thresholds for methotrexate, its location in her only remaining tube swings the balance toward salpingostomy to preserve fertility if the tube is salvageable; methotrexate risks tubal damage from the same-tube treated ectopic (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with the intention to perform left salpingectomy of the affected tube
options.rationale: Salpingectomy in the setting of a prior contralateral salpingectomy renders her surgically infertile requiring IVF; when the tube is salvageable, salpingostomy preserves an option (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with the intention to perform salpingostomy on the affected tube
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; RANZCOG guidance in a fertility conserving context favours salpingostomy over salpingectomy when the tube is salvageable and future conception depends on it (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Repeat serum beta hCG in 48 hours and observation with no immediate intervention
options.rationale: Static beta hCG (below the 50 percent decline that suggests failing pregnancy) with a visible adnexal mass in the setting of prior tubal ectopic requires active treatment rather than surveillance (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

options.text: Suction dilatation and curettage to confirm the pregnancy is not intrauterine before therapy
options.rationale: Ultrasound has already localised the pregnancy to the adnexa and a curettage risks disrupting a coexistent intrauterine pregnancy in a heterotopic case; imaging and beta hCG are sufficient here (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement).

explanation.summary: Choice between methotrexate, salpingostomy, and salpingectomy in tubal ectopic pregnancy depends on haemodynamic stability, beta hCG level, tubal mass size, presence of cardiac activity, and the woman's fertility priorities. RANZCOG considers methotrexate when beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, no significant pain, and reliable follow-up. Above 5000 IU/L or with rupture, surgery is required. The salpingostomy versus salpingectomy decision hinges on the state of the contralateral tube: with a normal contralateral tube salpingectomy is often chosen because recurrence in the treated tube is common, but with prior contralateral salpingectomy the balance flips toward preserving the only remaining tube.
key_points: Methotrexate threshold: beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm
No cardiac activity and no significant pain are also required
Prior contralateral salpingectomy flips choice to salpingostomy
Beta hCG must fall over 15 percent between day 4 and day 7 after methotrexate
Rupture, haemodynamic instability, or heterotopic pregnancy needs surgery
explanation.pearls: Persistent trophoblast rates after salpingostomy are around 8 percent; weekly beta hCG follow-up is mandatory until below 5 IU/L to detect and treat with methotrexate if plateau or rise.

subtopic_detail: Threatened preterm labour at 30 weeks with contraindications to nifedipine
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 26 year old G2P1 woman at 30+1 weeks gestation presents with 4 hours of regular painful contractions and a small amount of clear vaginal discharge. This pregnancy has been complicated by placenta praevia diagnosed on the 19 week morphology scan and confirmed on 28 week rescan; the placenta covers the internal os by 32 mm.

Her previous baby was born at 34 weeks after preterm labour. On examination her contractions are palpable every 4 minutes, lasting 45 seconds. Vital signs are pulse 96, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 with reactive CTG. Speculum examination reveals no visible cervical dilation but the cervical os is open to 1 finger tip on transvaginal ultrasound with cervical length 12 mm. Amniotic fluid pooling test is negative. Foetal fibronectin is positive.

She has no penicillin allergy, no antihypertensive requirement and has never taken a calcium channel blocker.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, FHR 148 with reactive CTG
data_table.Examination: Contractions every 4 minutes lasting 45 seconds; no vaginal bleeding; cervical length 12 mm on TVUS; foetal fibronectin positive
data_table.Antenatal history: Placenta praevia covering internal os by 32 mm, previous preterm birth at 34 weeks

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate tocolytic in addition to betamethasone and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection?

options.text: Atosiban intravenous loading dose then continuous infusion for up to 48 hours
options.rationale: Atosiban (oxytocin receptor antagonist) is preferred when nifedipine is contraindicated or undesirable; its neutral cardiovascular profile suits placenta praevia where haemodynamic changes could obscure obstetric haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally then 10 to 20 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours
options.rationale: Nifedipine is first-line tocolytic in AU practice but is not preferred here because it can drop blood pressure and mask the ongoing placenta praevia bleeding risk; another agent is preferred (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Salbutamol intravenous infusion titrated to reduce contraction frequency
options.rationale: Beta agonist tocolysis is no longer recommended in AU because of maternal cardiovascular adverse events including pulmonary oedema (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Indomethacin 100 mg per rectum then 25 mg orally every 6 hours for 48 hours
options.rationale: Indomethacin is avoided over 32 weeks and can cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus; at 30 weeks it is possible but the safety profile is inferior to atosiban with placenta praevia (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading as the primary tocolytic agent
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is used for foetal neuroprotection under 30 weeks, and no longer recommended as a tocolytic in isolation; her indication for magnesium is neuroprotection at the 30 week borderline (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement).
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

explanation.summary: Threatened preterm labour management aims for 48 hours of pregnancy prolongation to complete corticosteroids for lung maturation and magnesium sulfate for foetal neuroprotection under 30 weeks. Nifedipine is the AU first-line tocolytic, with atosiban preferred when nifedipine is contraindicated or where its vasodilator effect would obscure haemodynamic monitoring as in placenta praevia. Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM at 0 and 24 hours delivers full lung maturation, while magnesium neuroprotection uses a 4 g load then 1 g/h to birth or 24 hours. Beta agonists are no longer used because of maternal cardiovascular events.
key_points: Aim of tocolysis is 48 h to complete steroids and neuroprotection
Nifedipine is AU first-line tocolytic
Atosiban is preferred with placenta praevia or nifedipine contraindication
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses, 24 hours apart
Magnesium neuroprotection under 30 weeks
explanation.pearls: Foetal fibronectin is a bedside vaginal swab; a negative result under 30 weeks has a strong negative predictive value (over 95 percent for delivery within 7 days) and often permits discharge without tocolysis.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Labour and Birth Statement

subtopic_detail: Late onset FGR delivery timing with abnormal umbilical Doppler
stem:
You are the maternal foetal medicine registrar. A 30 year old G2P1 woman is at 36+4 weeks and has been under surveillance for a small for gestational age baby since a growth scan at 32 weeks showed estimated foetal weight on the 5th centile with a normal Doppler. Her first baby was born at term and weighed 3.4 kg.

Today her repeat scan shows estimated foetal weight on the 3rd centile with abdominal circumference on the less than 1st centile, umbilical artery pulsatility index at the 97th centile, and cerebroplacental ratio less than 1.0. Amniotic fluid volume is normal with a deepest vertical pocket of 3.2 cm. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is normal. CTG is reactive with a normal baseline of 138 beats per minute and no decelerations. Blood pressure today is 128/78 mmHg with no proteinuria; her booking blood pressure was 122/74 mmHg.

She has no other medical conditions and has completed her booking, morphology and antenatal blood tests without abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, no proteinuria, FHR 138 with reactive CTG
data_table.Ultrasound: EFW on 3rd centile, AC less than 1st centile, umbilical artery PI 97th centile, cerebroplacental ratio less than 1.0, AFI DVP 3.2 cm, MCA PSV normal
data_table.Antenatal history: Booking BP 122/74 mmHg, first baby term 3.4 kg, no medical conditions

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue outpatient twice weekly CTG and repeat Doppler in 7 days with no immediate change
options.rationale: A cerebroplacental ratio under 1.0 with rising umbilical artery PI reflects late onset placental insufficiency and is an indication for delivery beyond 36 weeks; conservative outpatient management risks stillbirth (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Deliver by induction of labour after a course of betamethasone commenced today
options.rationale: Late-onset FGR beyond 36 weeks with an abnormal Doppler (CPR under 1.0 or elevated umbilical artery PI) is an indication for delivery by induction of labour under RANZCOG; steroids can still be considered in some pathways though most deliver without further delay near term (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Elective caesarean section without a trial of labour for the small for gestational age foetus
options.rationale: Late-onset FGR with reactive CTG does not require caesarean by default; induction is the primary AU approach with intrapartum continuous CTG monitoring (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Admit for daily CTG and weekly Doppler and defer delivery until 39 weeks
options.rationale: Deferring delivery until 39 weeks in the presence of abnormal Doppler carries higher stillbirth risk than delivery near 37 weeks in this population; guidance recommends delivery from 36+0 (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline).

options.text: Start aspirin 150 mg daily and continue to 39 weeks with weekly ultrasound review
options.rationale: Aspirin is preventive and started before 16 weeks for those at risk of pre-eclampsia and FGR; starting at 36 weeks provides no benefit and delays needed delivery (Source: RANZCOG FGR Guideline; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline).

explanation.summary: Late-onset foetal growth restriction (after 32 weeks) is characterised by mild growth changes and subtle Doppler abnormalities and is associated with stillbirth risk. The Delphi consensus criteria (small for gestational age plus abnormal Doppler including a cerebroplacental ratio under 1.0 or umbilical artery pulsatility index above 95th centile) defines FGR versus constitutional smallness. RANZCOG recommends delivery by 37 weeks for late-onset FGR with abnormal Doppler; earlier if surveillance deteriorates. Route of delivery balances Doppler severity, CTG, and cervical favourability; induction with continuous CTG is appropriate with a reactive CTG and normal MCA PSV.
key_points: FGR needs SGA plus abnormal Doppler under Delphi consensus
CPR under 1.0 signals placental redistribution and stillbirth risk
Deliver at 36 to 37 weeks with abnormal Doppler
Induction with continuous CTG if surveillance and cervix allow
Aspirin is preventive before 16 weeks, not curative
explanation.pearls: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is used to screen for foetal anaemia rather than growth restriction; a value above 1.5 multiples of median suggests anaemia.

subtopic_detail: Severe OHSS after IVF requiring paracentesis versus admission
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman on day 9 after transvaginal oocyte retrieval. Her IVF cycle used a GnRH antagonist protocol with recombinant FSH 250 units daily; 32 oocytes were collected and she was triggered with hCG rather than a GnRH agonist because of a scheduling preference. She had a single fresh cleavage stage embryo transfer on day 3 and now presents with 4 days of progressive abdominal distension, breathlessness on climbing stairs, and reduced urine output.

On examination she is breathless at rest. Vital signs are pulse 118, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Abdominal examination shows a tense distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a palpable pelvic mass extending to the umbilicus. Bloods: haemoglobin 168 g/L (115-165), haematocrit 51 percent (36-46), white cells 18 x10^9/L (4-11), platelets 460 x10^9/L (150-400), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 24 g/L (35-50). Beta hCG is 320 IU/L; urine output over the last 6 hours is 60 mL.

Ultrasound confirms bilateral 12 cm enlarged ovaries with multiple follicular cysts and a moderate volume of free abdominal fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense distended abdomen, shifting dullness, palpable mass to the umbilicus
data_table.Ultrasound: Bilateral 12 cm ovaries with follicular cysts, moderate free abdominal fluid

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Immediate laparotomy and bilateral oophorectomy to remove the hyperstimulated enlarged ovaries
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for suspected ovarian torsion, cyst rupture with haemodynamic instability, or ectopic pregnancy; OHSS itself is medically managed and ovaries are preserved (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

options.text: Outpatient monitoring with high protein oral fluids and daily blood tests as ambulatory care
options.rationale: Severe OHSS with haematocrit over 45 percent, oliguria, hypoxia and hyponatraemia is not managed as an outpatient because of VTE and renal failure risk (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

options.text: Frusemide 40 mg intravenous bolus to increase urine output and reduce abdominal ascites volume
options.rationale: Diuretics in OHSS worsen intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration; the pathophysiology is third-spacing not fluid overload (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

options.text: Admit, commence intravenous crystalloid and human albumin, and arrange ultrasound guided paracentesis
options.rationale: This is severe OHSS with third-spacing (haematocrit 51 percent, oliguria, hyponatraemia, hypoxia, tense ascites) requiring inpatient management; RANZCOG-endorsed pathways use IV crystalloid then human albumin plus paracentesis for tense ascites and hypoxia (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement; RCOG OHSS Guideline).

options.text: Repeat beta hCG in 48 hours before deciding any further intervention or admission arrangements
options.rationale: Delaying intervention in severe OHSS to await beta hCG risks renal failure, VTE and ARDS; treatment does not depend on confirming pregnancy (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement).

explanation.summary: OHSS is an iatrogenic complication of ART with fluid shift into the third space driven by VEGF-mediated capillary leak. The syndrome is classified mild (abdominal distension), moderate (ultrasound ascites, ovaries over 5 cm), severe (clinical ascites, haematocrit over 45 percent, hyponatraemia, oliguria, hypoproteinaemia), or critical (tense ascites, ARDS, thromboembolism, renal failure). Severe OHSS needs admission, cautious IV fluid resuscitation (100 to 150 mL/h crystalloid then albumin 25 percent for volume expansion), VTE prophylaxis, and paracentesis for tense ascites and hypoxia. Diuretics are avoided because they worsen intravascular depletion. Pregnancy exacerbates OHSS through endogenous hCG and often prolongs the illness.
key_points: Severe OHSS: HCT over 45, oliguria, hyponatraemia, hypoxia
Third-spacing pathophysiology, not fluid overload
Avoid diuretics; use crystalloid then human albumin
Paracentesis for tense ascites and hypoxia
VTE prophylaxis is mandatory during admission
explanation.pearls: GnRH agonist trigger (leuprolide) instead of hCG substantially reduces severe OHSS risk; freezing all embryos avoids endogenous hCG stimulation from an early pregnancy that would worsen the syndrome.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 28 year old G3P2 woman with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 38+1 weeks has delivered a cephalic first twin (2.9 kg) after a 45 minute second stage. Her previous births were both singleton uncomplicated vaginal deliveries.

Sixteen minutes after the first birth the CTG on the second twin shows recurrent variable decelerations to 90 beats per minute lasting 40 seconds, and the baseline is 155 beats per minute. Bedside ultrasound reveals the second twin lying transverse with the back down (dorsoinferior). The membranes are intact and the estimated foetal weight is 2.6 kg. Vaginal examination reveals the cervix is fully dilated with no presenting part palpable. There is no cord felt.

The operating theatre is 3 minutes away and an epidural is running well. Vital signs are pulse 92, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 155 with recurrent variable decelerations. The consultant obstetrician is in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, FHR 155 with recurrent variable decelerations
data_table.Ultrasound: Second twin transverse lie with back down (dorsoinferior); intact membranes; EFW 2.6 kg
data_table.Examination: Cervix fully dilated, no presenting part palpable, no cord felt
data_table.Setting: Epidural in situ, theatre 3 minutes away, consultant obstetrician present

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in delivering the second twin?

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section with general anaesthesia for the second twin
options.rationale: Caesarean for a second twin after successful vaginal first twin birth increases combined maternal morbidity; a controlled internal podalic version with breech extraction achieves faster delivery when the operator is experienced (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: External cephalic version through the abdominal wall with tocolysis using intravenous salbutamol
options.rationale: ECV of the second twin has poor success in labour and delays delivery when the CTG is already non-reassuring; internal manoeuvres are preferred in this setting (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: Internal podalic version with breech extraction under epidural top up in the birthing room
options.rationale: In dichorionic diamniotic twins with a dorsoinferior transverse second twin and non-reassuring CTG in an experienced hands setting with epidural in situ, internal podalic version and breech extraction is safer and faster than caesarean and preserves the vaginal delivery pathway; the manoeuvre grasps the foetal feet and delivers as an assisted breech (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: Rupture membranes to allow the presenting part to descend then commence oxytocin
options.rationale: Rupturing membranes in a transverse lie risks cord prolapse and cannot achieve descent because no presenting part is engaged; the delivery pathway needs an actively directed foetal manipulation (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

options.text: Await spontaneous rotation for 30 minutes before intervening if the CTG remains reassuring
options.rationale: The CTG shows non-reassuring recurrent variable decelerations already; waiting extends foetal compromise and adds no likelihood of spontaneous rotation in a dorsoinferior transverse (Source: RANZCOG Twin Birth Statement).

explanation.summary: The Twin Birth Study established vaginal delivery of the second twin as safe when the first is cephalic and the second is under 4 kg, regardless of the second twin's presentation. Non-cephalic second twins may be delivered by internal podalic version and breech extraction, by breech extraction directly if breech, or by caesarean if the operator lacks experience with internal manoeuvres. Dorsoinferior transverse lie is particularly amenable to internal podalic version. The team must be ready to convert to caesarean if extraction fails, if cord prolapse occurs, or if maternal or foetal status deteriorates. Continuous CTG and adequate anaesthesia (epidural top up or general anaesthesia if needed) are essential.
key_points: Vaginal birth of second twin safe with cephalic first and EFW under 4 kg
Dorsoinferior transverse suits internal podalic version
Internal podalic version + breech extraction is fast in experienced hands
Ready to convert to caesarean for failure or deterioration
Rupturing membranes in transverse lie risks cord prolapse
explanation.pearls: For a dorsosuperior transverse (back up) second twin, internal podalic version is much harder because the operator's hand must sweep past the foetal back to reach the feet; caesarean is often the safer choice.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine metabolic and haematological monitoring at 4 weeks
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clozapine clinic. A 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine for 4 weeks after failing trials of risperidone and olanzapine. His dose has been titrated to 300 mg orally at night with weekly white cell counts remaining within normal limits.

He has gained 3 kg in 4 weeks and reports increased appetite and daytime drowsiness. He denies constipation. He smokes 15 cigarettes daily and drinks 4 standard drinks on Friday and Saturday nights. His mental state examination shows less prominent auditory hallucinations, improved sleep, and lifted mood. Vital signs are pulse 88, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Weight is 92 kg (baseline 89 kg), waist circumference 102 cm.

Baseline metabolic screen 4 weeks ago showed fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), HbA1c 5.4 percent (under 5.7 percent), total cholesterol 4.8 mmol/L (under 5.5), triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L (under 2.0). His most recent full blood count from 3 days ago is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 132/86 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Weight 92 kg (baseline 89 kg), waist 102 cm; MSE with reduced auditory hallucinations, lifted mood
data_table.Investigations 4 weeks ago (baseline): Fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), HbA1c 5.4% (<5.7%), total cholesterol 4.8 mmol/L (<5.5), triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L (<2.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next monitoring step?

options.text: Cease clozapine and reinitiate risperidone at his prior dose of 6 mg daily
options.rationale: Ceasing an effective clozapine trial after 4 weeks of response is not indicated for early weight gain; the switch back removes treatment resistant response (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Repeat metabolic bloods immediately today given the 3 kg weight gain
options.rationale: 3 months from initiation is the recommended interval; a 3 kg gain in 4 weeks warrants dietitian and exercise input but not immediate biochemistry (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Reduce clozapine dose to 200 mg orally at night for weight control
options.rationale: Dose reduction risks losing symptomatic benefit; weight gain is managed with lifestyle first and metformin as adjunct rather than dose reduction (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Repeat fasting lipids, fasting glucose and HbA1c at 3 months from clozapine start
options.rationale: RANZCP metabolic monitoring for clozapine repeats fasting glucose and lipids at 3 months from initiation, then 6 months, then annually; HbA1c at 3 months provides an early signal of insulin resistance (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Add ziprasidone 40 mg twice daily as adjunct to reduce metabolic burden
options.rationale: Polypharmacy adds side effects and pharmacokinetic interactions without evidence of metabolic benefit in clozapine users; the answer is lifestyle intervention plus scheduled monitoring (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Clozapine causes greater metabolic morbidity than any other antipsychotic (weight gain, insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia). RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines set a monitoring schedule: baseline fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, weight, waist, blood pressure; repeat at 3, 6 and 12 months, then annually. Weekly white cell counts continue for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly. Weight gain is common in the first 6 months and is managed with dietitian, exercise, and metformin if BMI or waist trend continues to rise. Do not stop or dose-reduce an effective clozapine trial for early weight gain alone.
key_points: Baseline plus 3, 6, 12 months then annual metabolic monitoring
Weekly WCC for 18 weeks, fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly
Manage weight with lifestyle then metformin, not dose reduction
Waist over 94 cm (male) or 80 cm (female) signals metabolic risk
Do not cease effective clozapine trial for early weight gain
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 mg orally titrated to 1 g twice daily is the evidence-based adjunct that limits antipsychotic weight gain; consider it when BMI increase exceeds 5 percent from baseline.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Long term lithium monitoring at 6 month review
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 47 year old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 900 mg daily for 2 years with good mood stabilisation and no relapses. Her most recent lithium level 3 months ago was 0.72 mmol/L. She takes no other medications, does not smoke, and drinks 3 standard drinks on weekends.

Today she attends for routine monitoring. She feels well with stable mood, no tremor, no polyuria, and no gastrointestinal upset. Her weight is unchanged from baseline. Vital signs are pulse 74, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Her general physical examination is unremarkable.

Her general practitioner has already arranged today's blood tests: lithium level, urea and electrolytes, creatinine, TSH, and adjusted calcium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.History: Bipolar I; lithium 900 mg daily for 2 years; no relapses; last lithium 0.72 mmol/L three months ago
data_table.Symptoms: Well, no tremor, no polyuria, no GI upset; weight unchanged

lead_in: Which single set of monitoring blood tests is minimally required at this 6 monthly review under Australian guidance?

options.text: Lithium level with urea and electrolytes and creatinine only
options.rationale: Long-term lithium monitoring requires thyroid function testing every 6 to 12 months because of the risk of hypothyroidism; omitting TSH misses a common preventable morbidity (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Lithium level with 24 hour urine collection for urinary lithium and osmolality
options.rationale: A 24 hour collection is reserved for evaluation of polyuria or suspected nephrogenic diabetes insipidus rather than routine monitoring in an asymptomatic patient (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Lithium level with liver function tests and full blood count only
options.rationale: Liver function testing is not part of routine lithium monitoring (lithium is renally excreted); this set misses TSH, calcium and renal indices (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Lithium level and TSH only every 12 months without renal or calcium tests
options.rationale: Renal monitoring (U&E, creatinine, eGFR) is central because lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy; adjusted calcium screens for parathyroid effect (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Lithium level with urea and electrolytes, creatinine, TSH and adjusted calcium
options.rationale: Australian bipolar guidance recommends 6-monthly lithium level, U&E, creatinine and TSH, with adjusted calcium every 6 to 12 months to detect lithium associated hyperparathyroidism (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

explanation.summary: Lithium remains a first line mood stabiliser in bipolar I disorder with clear anti-suicide effect. Long-term monitoring requires attention to the renal (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic tubular disease, eGFR trend), thyroid (up to 15 percent develop hypothyroidism), and parathyroid (10 percent develop hyperparathyroidism) systems. Australian guidance repeats lithium level, U&E, creatinine and TSH every 6 months and adjusted calcium every 6 to 12 months once stable. Target lithium is typically 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance; higher (0.8 to 1.0) for acute mania under supervision. Toxicity presents with coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, and vomiting; level above 1.5 mmol/L is toxic.
key_points: 6 monthly: lithium level, U&E, creatinine, TSH
6 to 12 monthly: adjusted calcium for hyperparathyroidism
Target maintenance level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L
Toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting
Level above 1.5 mmol/L is toxic and needs intervention
explanation.pearls: Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism raises PTH and calcium but the patient is often asymptomatic; screen adjusted calcium routinely because early detection allows medication review before parathyroidectomy is needed.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial management of catatonia in the acute ward
stem:
You are the on call psychiatry registrar in a general hospital. A 24 year old woman with a 2 year history of schizoaffective disorder has been admitted for a manic relapse and has been in the ward for 5 days. Her regular olanzapine has been withheld for the last 48 hours because of poor oral intake.

The nurses call you because for the last 12 hours she has been mute, immobile, and holds any position her limbs are placed in for over 60 seconds without falling. She resists passive movement of both arms with an equal counter-force to the applied force. She does not blink to visual threat. Vital signs are pulse 108, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Bedside investigations: capillary glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), CRP 4 mg/L (under 10), CK 210 U/L (25-190), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145).

She is drinking sips of water only when the cup is placed to her lips. She has no evidence of infection on chest, abdominal or urinary examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility for over 60 seconds, gegenhalten with passive movement, no blink to threat
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), CRP 4 mg/L (<10), CK 210 U/L (25-190), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Restart olanzapine 10 mg orally today to treat the underlying schizoaffective disorder
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome; catatonia is treated first before restarting antipsychotic (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscular as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge with reassessment at 30 minutes
options.rationale: Catatonia (waxy flexibility, mutism, gegenhalten, staring) responds to benzodiazepines; a lorazepam 2 mg IM challenge produces observable improvement in most catatonia and confirms the diagnosis while treating it (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenous over 30 minutes for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS is unlikely because she is afebrile with normal CK and stable haemodynamics; the presentation is catatonia and dantrolene is not first-line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Sodium valproate 20 mg/kg intravenous loading dose for suspected non-convulsive status
options.rationale: There is no EEG or clinical evidence of ongoing seizure and the clinical picture (waxy flexibility, gegenhalten) is catatonia rather than non-convulsive status (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular as chemical restraint for acute behavioural disturbance
options.rationale: First-generation antipsychotics carry a high risk of precipitating malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome in this setting; the priority is benzodiazepine challenge not chemical restraint (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor disturbance defined by 3 of 12 DSM-5 features including stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, or echopraxia. Half of cases occur in mood disorders (especially mania and depression), a quarter in psychotic disorders, and the remainder in medical or neurological illness. First line treatment is benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM or IV, repeated 3 to 6 hourly to a total 8 to 16 mg/day); response is often dramatic within hours. Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis) requires ECT. Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia has resolved.
key_points: Catatonia: 3 of 12 DSM-5 features including waxy flexibility, mutism
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM as diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves
Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability) needs ECT
Screen for medical causes: encephalitis, metabolic, autoimmune
explanation.pearls: The Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is the AU-used screen; 2 of the first 14 items or a total score at least 6 supports diagnosis and quantifies severity for treatment response.

subtopic_detail: Amitriptyline overdose with widened QRS in the emergency department
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 32 year old woman is brought in by ambulance 2 hours after an impulsive ingestion of 40 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (total 1000 mg) taken with wine. She has a background of major depressive disorder and has been prescribed amitriptyline for chronic migraine prevention.

On arrival she is drowsy with GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5). Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96 percent on 4 L/min oxygen by nasal prongs, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. She has dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils and diminished bowel sounds. Twelve lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 128, QRS duration 132 milliseconds (under 120), R wave in aVR 5 mm (under 3 mm), and a QT interval of 460 milliseconds.

Capillary glucose is 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-7.7). Venous blood gas shows pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). She is on continuous cardiac monitoring and intravenous access is established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 96% on 4 L/min O2, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3V4M5), dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils, diminished bowel sounds
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia 128, QRS 132 ms (<120), R wave aVR 5 mm (>3), QT 460 ms
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), venous pH 7.32 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-32), Na 140 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 100 mmol intravenous bolus over 1 to 2 minutes with monitoring
options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by sodium channel blockade; QRS over 100 ms is the threshold to give hypertonic sodium bicarbonate and R in aVR over 3 mm confirms significant blockade (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube with sorbitol for gut decontamination
options.rationale: At 2 hours post ingestion charcoal has limited efficacy, and giving oral charcoal in a drowsy patient without airway protection risks aspiration; treat the toxicity first (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute then infusion
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiotoxicity where sodium bicarbonate has failed; first-line intervention for QRS widening is sodium bicarbonate (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

options.text: Flecainide 100 mg intravenous over 10 minutes to normalise the widened QRS complex
options.rationale: Flecainide is a class Ic sodium channel blocker and worsens TCA cardiotoxicity; class I antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

options.text: Physostigmine 2 mg intravenous over 5 minutes as a specific antimuscarinic antagonist
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate asystole and seizure by unopposed cholinergic effect combined with sodium channel blockade (Source: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus

explanation.summary: TCA overdose is a leading cause of drug related death from prescribed medications. Amitriptyline and dothiepin have the highest cardiotoxicity because of sodium channel blockade in ventricular myocardium, which widens QRS, produces R wave in aVR, and predisposes to broad complex tachyarrhythmia. Central effects include coma, seizures, and anticholinergic delirium. QRS over 100 ms indicates significant sodium channel blockade and the threshold for hypertonic sodium bicarbonate to keep pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS under 120. Class I antiarrhythmics and physostigmine are contraindicated; seizures are treated with benzodiazepines rather than phenytoin.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms is threshold for sodium bicarbonate
R wave in aVR over 3 mm confirms significant Na channel block
Alkalinise to pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS under 120 ms
Class I antiarrhythmics and physostigmine are contraindicated
Benzodiazepines first-line for seizures; avoid phenytoin
explanation.pearls: The R wave in aVR sign is more specific than QRS width: R at least 3 mm or R:S ratio at least 0.7 predicts seizure and arrhythmia risk and may justify treatment even with a borderline QRS.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Toxinology Consensus
